tldr_text:
Stephen Miller pledged loyalty to President Donald Trump during a Friday evening appearance at Mar-a-Lago, following Trump's announcement that Miller will become the next White House chief of staff on Monday, November 9, 2026. Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, replaces Susie Wiles, who submitted her resignation on Thursday night after serving in the position throughout Trump's second term.

Russian military forces launched thirty-six ballistic missiles and one hundred seventy-two strike drones overnight across twelve Ukrainian regions, heavily targeting the capital of Kyiv. The bombardment injured at least nine people across the country, including a child, and partially destroyed a kindergarten in the Solomianskyi district. Explosions also hit the 816-meter Northern Bridge spanning the Dnipro River, forcing municipal authorities to close the route to traffic in both directions.

Five people were killed and more than a dozen others injured on Saturday afternoon when a gunman drove a car into the Main Market Square in Krakow, Poland, and began firing at random people. Police officers confronted the shooter at the scene and shot him during the arrest. The suspect returned fire during the encounter, injuring two police officers among the wounded.

President Donald Trump stated in the Oval Office that he will soon decide whether to launch new military strikes against Iran or pursue a deal to end the eight-month conflict. The administration faces conflicting pressures following midterm elections in which Democrats captured control of both the House and Senate and gained a majority of governorships.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces a bipartisan impeachment vote scheduled in the House of Representatives next week, following the introduction of articles of impeachment by Representative Thomas Massie, Republican of Kentucky. Massie announced plans to bring the resolution charging Hegseth with high crimes and misdemeanors to the floor on Monday or Tuesday, stating that congressional support for Hegseth's removal has expanded since the midterm elections.

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot secured recommendations from 67 parliamentarians to form Israel's next governing coalition, surpassing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who received 46 recommendations. Israeli President Isaac Herzog will announce on Sunday which political figure receives the mandate to form a government, following two days of consultations with political factions in the 120 seat Knesset.
audio_script:
## COLD
A: Three days after the Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress, the White House has a new chief of staff. He's the architect of the administration's immigration enforcement.

## TITLE
A: From Void News, this is On Air. It's Saturday, November seventh.
B: Today: Stephen Miller takes the chief of staff's office on Monday, and the reaction splits along party lines before he's sat down. Then overnight, thirty-six Russian ballistic missiles over Ukraine, and a bridge in Kyiv closed in both directions.

## LEAD | Miller Takes the West Wing
A: On Friday, President Donald Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. It takes effect on Monday, November ninth. Miller's the deputy chief of staff right now. On Friday evening he was at Mar-a-Lago, and he pledged loyalty to the president.
A: Wiles had held the post since the start of this term, and she was the first woman to hold it. She submitted her resignation on Thursday night. According to the president's announcement, she's moving to his political operation.
A: The appointment lands three days after the midterms. Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress. They dropped at least forty-four House seats and seven Senate seats. And there's a number that sits behind it: a Fox News exit survey found fifty-eight percent of voters believed federal immigration enforcement had gone too far. Miller is the person most identified with that enforcement.
B: That record runs across both terms. Miller's forty-one, and he's been a central architect of the administration's immigration actions. That's the zero-tolerance border policy of twenty eighteen, the travel restrictions on several Muslim-majority nations, and an executive push directing Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest three thousand people a day. Congress backed that enforcement with about one hundred seventy billion dollars under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, passed in July of last year.
A: The reaction has split sharply, and along party lines. Pete Hegseth and the former congressman Matt Gaetz publicly backed the move. The incoming House majority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, called Miller a dangerous extremist with American blood on his hands, and urged the president to reverse the appointment. And it's not only Democrats: Republican critics and business sectors expressed concern about Miller's focus on hardline enforcement after Tuesday's results.
B: The outlets differ on what the story is. The Daily Beast and CNN emphasise internal West Wing infighting and factional tensions, and they liken the environment to the administration's early turmoil. The Daily Wire and The Daily Caller focus on the official resignation statements and on praise from administration figures. The Daily Beast also reported behind-the-scenes lobbying calls by Katie Miller, urging Trump allies to back her husband for the post. The Associated Press and RTE didn't address that account.
B: The Washington Post framed the appointment around pushback from industries facing enforcement pressure. Newsweek and The Hill led with Miller's remarks at Mar-a-Lago, declaring the Republican Party stronger than ever. Of the sixty outlets Void placed on this story, twenty-four sit left of centre, twenty at the centre and sixteen right of it.

## SECOND | Kyiv Under Fire Before Talks
B: In Kyiv, the night brought the heaviest of a wider assault. Russian forces launched thirty-six ballistic missiles and one hundred seventy-two strike drones across twelve Ukrainian regions. At least nine people were injured across the country, including a child. A kindergarten in the Solomianskyi district was partially destroyed.
B: Explosions hit the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, a span of about eight hundred and sixteen metres. The city closed it to traffic in both directions. The strikes damaged energy infrastructure and caused power and water disruptions in the capital. The mayor, Vitali Klitschko, says municipal workers have started repairs, and water pressure and heating in the capital were partially restored. Elsewhere, three consecutive strikes hit a Naftogaz oil and gas facility in central Ukraine and set off a large fire. The company's acting chairman, Serhiy Fedorenko, says the fire was contained with no staff casualties.
B: The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed the strikes. It says the operation targeted Ukraine's military-industrial production, energy installations and transport networks. And the timing matters: the assault came just before scheduled trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi, with delegations from Russia, Ukraine and the United States, aimed at ending the war.
A: The coverage splits on what was hit. Ukrainian outlets and officials detailed civilian casualties and damage to homes, kindergartens and municipal utilities. Russian state coverage focused exclusively on military and industrial targets, including the Meridian missile plant and the Tripolskaya thermal power station. Local Ukrainian reports tracked damage in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv and Dnipro, while the international wires centred on the capital and the Abu Dhabi talks. Of the twenty-one outlets Void placed on this story, six sit left of centre, thirteen at the centre and two right of it.

## DESK
A: The rest of the desk.
A: In Krakow, a gunman drove a car into the Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon and fired at random. Five people were killed. Reports of the injured range from ten to more than a dozen, two police officers among them. Police shot and arrested him.
B: President Trump says he'll soon decide whether to launch new strikes against Iran or pursue a deal to end the eight-month conflict. Vice President JD Vance has blamed the Republican losses on the war, high costs and support for Israel. Oil traded near ninety dollars a barrel.
A: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces an impeachment vote in the House next week, after Representative Thomas Massie introduced articles against him. The House Oversight chairman, James Comer, declined to endorse Hegseth on Saturday. The president says he keeps his confidence in Hegseth.
B: In Israel, sixty-seven members of parliament recommended the opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government, against forty-six for Benjamin Netanyahu. President Isaac Herzog announces the mandate on Sunday. Once tasked, Eisenkot will have twenty-eight days to negotiate a coalition.
A: Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate race in Michigan, fifty-two percent to forty-six, over the Republican Mike Rogers. He becomes the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He has named Brenda Abdelall as his transition director.
B: Several incoming Democratic senators say they won't support Chuck Schumer for majority leader. Schumer states he has sufficient votes within his caucus to retain his leadership position. The president says Schumer probably secures the position.
A: The United States carried out limited airstrikes on Iranian air defense systems on Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media confirmed two projectile impacts. United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations reports commercial vessel traffic sixty-five percent below pre-conflict levels.
B: Across Europe, coordinated bomb hoaxes targeted news organizations and passenger flights. Ireland's national broadcaster, RTE, evacuated its Dublin headquarters, and at least thirty-five aircraft were targeted this week. Investigators found no explosives and no injuries.

## OPINION | The Door Miller Will Hold
A: This is Void Opinion. Through a progressive lens today. The door Stephen Miller will hold.
A: Three days after the Republican Party lost at least forty-four House seats and seven Senate seats, the president named Stephen Miller White House chief of staff. Miller is the central architect of the administration's immigration actions across both terms: the zero-tolerance border policy of 2018, travel restrictions on several Muslim-majority nations, and an executive push directing Immigration and Customs Enforcement to arrest three thousand people a day, backed by about one hundred seventy billion dollars under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
A: Ask who bears the cost of that structure and who was asked. A Fox News exit survey found fifty-eight percent of voters believed federal immigration enforcement had gone too far. The voters answered on Tuesday. The appointment came on Friday.
A: We think the question is not Miller's character but what the office now rewards. Republican critics and business sectors have already expressed concern about his focus on hardline enforcement after the results. The incoming House majority leader, Hakeem Jeffries, urged the president to reverse the appointment. The Daily Beast reported lobbying calls by Katie Miller urging allies to back her husband; the Associated Press and RTE did not address that account.
A: A chief of staff decides who reaches the president. On Monday, the person most identified with the policy a majority of voters rejected will hold that door. The Congress that meets him in January is one his party no longer controls. That is the check the structure left standing.

## CLOSE
A: That's On Air from Void News. On Monday, Stephen Miller walks into the chief of staff's office; the Congress that meets him in January is one his party no longer controls. Every source, every story, at Void News.
